excerpt: Down at Puntan Flores, long before the war rewrote the Pacific, Japanese engineers poured concrete seaplane ramps to connect Yokohama to the south. Decades later—after the air raids, the CIA, and the jungle took over—the drains still carry the rain straight to the lagoon. A reflection on craftsmanship, memory, and what remains when empires pack up and leave.
author: Lexi Zotomayor
bodyText:
There is something curious about how well men used to pour concrete. Down at Puntan Flores, on the northern hip of Saipan where the land slopes gently into the lagoon, the Japanese laid down seaplane ramps and drainage troughs in the middle of the 1930s. They built them to last, mixing stone and sand with a deliberate, painstaking care that seems almost gentle when set against what came after. If you walk through Lower Base today—past the hum of the power plant and the tangle of tropical scrub—you can still find those drains. They are clear, level, and after ninety years of salt air and torrential rain, they still carry water away precisely as they were drawn to do.

At the first Marianas History Conference a few years back, David G. DeFant, an archaeologist who has spent a good deal of time taking the measure of old stones across Micronesia, brought along some slides of the site. He spoke of the surviving work with the professional affection one reserves for solid craftsmanship. "Remarkable," he called it. The concrete poured in 1934 had none of the frantic, slapdash quality of the bunkers thrown up in early 1944 when the American fleet was already on the horizon. The early structures belonged to a different mind, and a different tempo of living.

History in this corner of the Pacific is often told in sudden, violent bursts, but the story of Puntan Flores began in prose, not poetry. By 1910, under the League of Nations mandate, the port was already humming with Japanese commercial traffic. Sugar and commerce brought people—tens of thousands of Okinawan families moving south to work the fields, until the foreign population swelled from a couple hundred under the Germans to nearly sixty thousand by the late 1930s.

![Punta Flores](/assets/uploads/cms/puntan-flores.jpeg)

When the seaplane base was laid out in 1934, it was fundamentally a civilian affair, a maritime outpost connecting Yokohama to Saipan, Palau, Chuuk, and Jaluit. Double-engined Kawanishi flying boats operated by Dai Nippon Koku drifted down into the calm waters of the bay, bringing mail, cargo, and passengers on a schedule that felt permanent and peaceful. There were subtle arguments in Geneva and Washington about whether Japan was surreptitiously militarizing the mandate islands, arguments that eventually prompted Tokyo to walk out of the League of Nations altogether. Yet on the ground at Puntan Flores, the work remained thorough, orderly, and largely unhurried.

Then, as it always does when nations prepare for war, the rhythm shifted. Around 1939, the military assumed control. What had been a single concrete ramp grew into a sprawling warren of sixty-five buildings: steel hangars, semi-underground ammunition magazines, fuel bunkers, and nine arched air-raid shelters. But you could read the coming urgency in the masonry itself. The later additions lacked the finesse of the early work; the fine edges disappeared, replaced by rough aggregate and hurried forms.

When the invasion came in June 1944, the island changed hands, but the geography remained stubbornly useful. The Americans took Puntan Flores, widened the aprons to hold their heavier, clumsier aircraft, and converted the Japanese fuel bunker into a high-standing communications tower. Decades later, when the CIA set up its clandestine Naval Technical Training Unit on the heights of Capitol Hill, the heights became known simply as the "Upper Base," and the old Japanese seaplane ramp below inherited the utilitarian name it carries today: Lower Base.

DeFant noted, with a scholar’s soft regret, that almost everything we know about Puntan Flores comes from wartime intelligence dossiers—documents that tend to reduce complex human landscapes to targets, fuel capacities, and troop strength. They leave out the Japanese engineers who calculated the pitch of those drains, and the local hands who hauled the aggregate under a hot equatorial sun.

It is easy to look at an overgrown strip of concrete and see only a ruin of war. But if you stand by the water's edge at Puntan Flores long enough, past the rusting pipes and industrial clutter, you realize you are looking at a ledger of human ambition. The wars came and went, the empires dissolved, and the CIA packed up its filing cabinets and went home. What remains, half-buried under the morning-glory vines, is the smooth, solid curve of an old Japanese drainage ditch—still straight, still square, and still doing its modest job, waiting for the rain.
title: The Seaplanes of Puntan Flores
